Why, for an angled packing pad

Best fatigue resistance, least creep and the best tear strength of the eight — and tear strength matters here, because an internal corner is where an angled section splits. Not for oil, and it perishes in prolonged sunlight
Where the pad is exposed to weather or sees oil. Good fatigue life and reasonable tear strength, with better ozone resistance than natural rubber
Low-cost enclosed packing. Fatigue and tear below natural rubber, and no oil resistance
Weather, ozone and steam. Creeps more than natural rubber, so allow for it in the deflection
Where the pad sits in oil. Poor ozone resistance, so not for an exposed corner
Lowest tear strength of the eight, and an internal corner is a tear origin. Specify only where temperature leaves no choice
Expensive sealing compounds with no fatigue, creep or tear advantage in a packing pad
It packs and locates at the same time
The flat leg holds the gap; the upstand stops the assembly creeping sideways and protects the corner. A flat pad does the first job only — which is the whole reason to choose this shape.
Rubber does not cure at the angle you cut

Shrinkage pulls the two legs against each other, so a cavity cut at 90° does not reliably give a part at 90°. We cut the tool with compensation and give the angle a stated tolerance — because a pad two degrees out bears on an edge, not a face.
The inside corner is where it fails
An internal angle concentrates stress, and a square root is where a flexing section splits first. We radius it in the tool, and we rank compounds on tear strength as well as on load.
One leg carries load and the other locates — they rarely need the same section. Tell us what each leg does and we will set them independently rather than moulding a uniform angle and hoping.

What is the minimum order quantity for this part?

We supply in bulk. The minimum run is 10,000 pieces per part number, per compound — or quoted per metre where the section is extruded, since the minimum then follows the die rather than the piece. Prototype and first-article lots sit outside the minimum.
Can you match a competitor specification or reverse-engineer an existing part?

Yes — and measure the angle on the part before you send it. Sections come out of some tools a degree or two off, and if the incumbent was out of square the assembly has usually been shimmed to suit. We work from the corner it has to sit in, not from the part that has been packing it.
What file formats do you accept for drawings?

PDF, DWG and DXF. A dimensioned section is enough — angle, both leg lengths and both leg thicknesses, with the inside radius if you have a preference. Add the load on each leg and hardness becomes our output rather than your input.
Do you provide material test reports with each shipment?

Yes. Material test reports, dimensional inspection sheets and a certificate of conformance ship with every consignment. Hardness, tensile to ASTM D412 and compression set to ASTM D395 Method B are tested in-house, and the included angle is gauged on every batch.
What are your payment and delivery terms for international orders?

TT and LC accepted, discussed per order. Ex-works Nashik or FOB Nhava Sheva. Commercial invoice, packing list and certificate of origin are issued with every consignment. Sections ship nested and unloaded.
